analysis.one_liner: Bans private prisons, reinstates federal parole, and caps what inmates pay for phone calls and money transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and no committee action, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended government contracts with private prison companies within two years, and given states the same deadline. It would have brought back federal parole for people sentenced after January 1, 2017, letting prisoners seek release after serving part of their term. It also would have capped what inmates and their families pay for prison phone calls and money transfers, ended the requirement that immigration authorities keep at least 34,000 detention beds, and banned detaining immigrant families. It was introduced by Senator Sanders, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a single cosponsor, and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Incarcerated people and their families, who pay high fees for phone calls and money transfers to stay in touch; federal prisoners who would become eligible for parole; and immigration detainees, who could qualify for community-based supervision instead of detention.

how_it_helps.text: Federal, state, and local governments would have had to take direct operational control of adult prisons and detention facilities within two years, with a possible one-year waiver, ending contracts with private prison companies.

Federal parole would have been reestablished for prisoners sentenced on or after January 1, 2017, with eligibility generally after serving one-third of the sentence and review hearings at set intervals.

The Federal Communications Commission would have set maximum rates for prison phone and video calls, required providers to offer collect and debit calling, and restricted the commission payments and extra fees that drive up costs for inmates' families.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would have set standards requiring that fees for sending money to inmates be reasonable and proportional to the actual cost of the service.

The requirement to maintain at least 34,000 immigration detention beds would have been eliminated, detention capacity would be set by actual need, and DHS would have had to build nationwide alternatives-to-detention programs and end family detention, including banning separating families to detain one member.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison operators, prison phone and video providers, and money-transfer companies would lose guaranteed revenue; federal and state governments would bear the cost of taking facilities back in-house and running a new parole system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison, prison phone, and money-transfer companies

drawbacks.text: Governments would have had two years (with a possible one-year waiver) to take over facilities and rehire or retrain staff, a costly transition for taxpayers at both the federal and state level.

Reinstated parole would have allowed earlier release for some federal prisoners, a change critics could reasonably argue affects public safety, and would have required funding a permanent Parole Commission.
The bill gave the Attorney General a waiver allowing continued private operation for up to one extra year, softening its own two-year deadline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people affected — inmates, detainees, and especially their families paying phone and money-transfer fees — the potential gains were large and concrete, since prisoners are a captive market with no ability to shop for a cheaper provider. The costs are real too: bringing prisons back in-house is expensive, and public operation is not a guarantee of humane conditions. The parole piece was the most ambitious and the most debatable, since earlier release trades prison costs against public-safety judgment calls. The bill's breadth also worked against it — it bundled privatization, sentencing, immigration detention, and telecom regulation into one measure that never attracted another senator's support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never received a cosponsor, and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on September 17, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison operators and the companies selling phone, video, and money-transfer services to inmates kept their contracts and fee revenue. Immigration authorities also kept the 34,000-bed detention requirement that the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison and prison services companies

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case that core imprisonment services should be run by government rather than contracted out.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral; the committee never held a markup or vote on it during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Private prison companies
against.role: Operators of for-profit prisons and detention centers
against.what_they_did: The industry's federal and state contracts were the direct target of the bill; it had no cosponsors and died without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split can be measured; it had one sponsor, an independent, and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Private prison operators (CoreCivic, GEO Group and similar)
industries.note: The bill would have phased out government contracts with private prisons within two years, removing the industry's core revenue stream. Its business depends on charging governments per occupied bed, so every person kept behind bars is a source of profit.

The bill would have let the FCC cap per-minute rates, ban or limit the commissions these companies pay prison administrators, and limit extra fees. Families of inmates currently bear those costs to stay in contact with loved ones.
The bill would have required the CFPB to set standards so fees for sending money to inmates are proportional to actual cost, curbing the high fees charged on a captive customer base.
Taking prison operations back in-house would have shifted work from contractors to public-sector corrections staff.
